reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal recessive cholestatic disorders presenting in infancy or early childhood with progressive cholestasis, intractable pruritus, and failure to thrive
PFIC type 1 (ATP8B1/FIC1) and type 2 (ABCB11/BSEP) characteristically show a low or normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase despite marked cholestasis
PFIC type 3 (ABCB4/MDR3) shows a raised gamma-glutamyl transferase because impaired biliary phospholipid secretion damages the bile duct epithelium
FIC1 disease is a systemic defect and may be accompanied by diarrhoea, pancreatitis, and sensorineural hearing loss beyond the liver
BSEP deficiency carries a significant risk of hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma, warranting tumour surveillance
Serum bile acids are markedly elevated while serum cholesterol is often normal or low, helping distinguish PFIC from other paediatric liver disease
Management centres on relieving pruritus, nutritional support with fat-soluble vitamins, ileal bile acid transport inhibitors or biliary diversion, and liver transplantation for end-stage disease
reference.pathophysiology: PFIC comprises several inherited defects in hepatocyte proteins that maintain bile formation and flow. FIC1 (ATP8B1) is an aminophospholipid flippase whose loss disrupts the canalicular membrane; BSEP (ABCB11) is the main bile salt export pump, so its failure traps bile acids inside hepatocytes; and MDR3 (ABCB4) translocates phosphatidylcholine into bile, so its deficiency yields bile that is toxic to the biliary tree. In each case impaired bile acid secretion produces intracellular accumulation of bile acids, hepatocyte injury, and progressive cholestasis that evolves to fibrosis and cirrhosis. The characteristic difference in gamma-glutamyl transferase reflects whether the underlying lesion damages the bile duct epithelium (high, as in MDR3 disease) or not (low or normal, as in FIC1 and BSEP disease).
additionalDifferentials: Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis (a milder allelic condition)
additionalInvestigations: Serum bile acids, bilirubin fractions, and gamma-glutamyl transferase to define the cholestatic pattern
Molecular genetic testing of ATP8B1, ABCB11, ABCB4 and related genes
Liver biopsy with immunostaining for BSEP and MDR3 and assessment of fibrosis
Fat-soluble vitamin levels and coagulation studies to gauge malabsorption
Abdominal ultrasound and cholangiography to exclude biliary obstruction and atresia
Alpha-fetoprotein and imaging surveillance for hepatobiliary malignancy in BSEP disease
redFlags: Rapidly progressive jaundice with coagulopathy indicating hepatic decompensation
Rising alpha-fetoprotein or a hepatic mass suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma in BSEP deficiency
Severe intractable pruritus with sleep disruption and self-mutilation
Growth failure and signs of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency such as bleeding or rickets
reference.prognosis: Without intervention most subtypes progress to biliary cirrhosis and liver failure during childhood, though disease-modifying therapy such as ileal bile acid transport inhibitors, surgical biliary diversion, and liver transplantation can markedly improve outcomes. BSEP disease additionally carries a lifelong risk of hepatobiliary malignancy requiring surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing a normal or low gamma-glutamyl transferase to a benign process rather than recognising low-GGT cholestasis of FIC1/BSEP disease
Overlooking extrahepatic features of FIC1 disease such as diarrhoea, pancreatitis, and hearing loss
Failing to institute malignancy surveillance in BSEP deficiency
Neglecting aggressive fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and nutritional support
Assuming liver transplantation cures FIC1 disease, since extrahepatic manifestations and post-transplant steatohepatitis or diarrhoea may persist
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
management: Ileal bile acid transporter inhibitors such as odevixibat or maralixibat to interrupt enterohepatic bile acid recycling and reduce pruritus and hepatocellular bile acid load
Ursodeoxycholic acid, which is especially beneficial in the ABCB4 (MDR3/PFIC3) form
Aggressive pruritus control with rifampicin, bile acid sequestrants and other antipruritics
Nutritional rehabilitation with medium-chain-triglyceride-based feeds and fat-soluble vitamin replacement, monitoring growth and coagulation
Surgical biliary diversion for symptom relief and disease modification, with liver transplantation for decompensated disease
Alpha-fetoprotein and imaging surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma in BSEP (PFIC2) disease
Genetic counselling and cascade testing for this autosomal recessive condition
